data.title: Missouri asks Supreme Court to restore GOP-friendly congressional map
data.description:
Missouri launched an effort at the Supreme Court late Friday to restore its Republican-friendly congressional map, warning that a lower ruling invalidating it has unleashed “unprecedented chaos” on the midterms. 

“A federal-election-administration disaster is unfolding in Missouri,” Missouri Attorney General Catherine Hanaway’s (R) office wrote in its emergency application.

Missouri’s new congressional map created a 7-1 GOP split by weakening Rep. Emanuel Cleaver’s (D-Mo.) Kansas City-based seat. It was one of a handful of states where Republicans have boosted their chances in the mid-decade redistricting war, adding to gains in places like Texas and Florida. 

On Thursday, the Missouri Supreme Court blocked the map. The court unanimously ruled that the state’s constitution permits voters to organize a referendum on the redistricting plan. Missouri Secretary of State Denny Hoskins (R) previously denied such an effort by deciding otherwise. 

The new ruling means Missouri cannot use its Republican-friendly map that it used for the primary. Instead, the state must revert to a 6-1 GOP-favored design. The referendum would be placed on the ballot for approval in November, but it can’t take effect, since voters haven’t signed off. 

“Only this Court can prevent Missouri from being forced to disenfranchise hundreds of thousands of voters; and only this Court can ensure that Missouri hosts a timely and lawful federal congressional election. The Court should do so,” the state wrote in court filings.

The case is on the Supreme Court’s emergency docket, where the court handles urgent matters on an expedited timeline, often without oral argument. By default, the request heads to Justice Brett Kavanaugh, an appointee of former President Trump who handles emergency matters arising from Missouri. He could also refer the case to the full court for a vote. 

Missouri argues the lower decision violated the federal Constitution, which hands state legislatures authority to regulate elections.

Hanaway’s office called the ruling “bizarre and profoundly anti-democratic” and said it would irreparably harm voters. 

“As far as Missouri is aware, no State has ever been forced to use a different congressional map for an election cycle merely because a small minority of voters submitted a petition. And it certainly has never been done after a completed primary election,” the state wrote. 

It lurches the Supreme Court into the redistricting wars once again. Last December, the high court revived a congressional map in Texas that sparked the mid-decade redistricting war by adding up to five Republican pickup opportunities. A lower court had invalidated it as a likely racial gerrymander. 

In May, the court refused Virginia Democrats’ plea to reinstate their congressional map after the state’s top court ruled they hadn’t followed procedures mandated by Virginia’s constitution. 

And on its normal docket, the Supreme Court earlier this year narrowed redistricting challenges under Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act. That decision has allowed states like Louisiana to change their maps ahead of the midterms.

data.title: Democrats seek to counter RNC's 'Trump-a-palooza' convention in Dallas
data.description:
Democrats are seeking to seize on the Republican National Committee’s first-of-its-kind midterm convention with plans for counterprogramming around the two-day Dallas bash as the party eyes a Senate flip in the red state. 

Republicans are hopeful the so-called “Trump-a-palooza” next week excites the base about turning out amid a bleak midterm outlook for the GOP and concerns about low attendance, timing and President Trump’s approval rating. The toss-up Senate race in Texas, where Trump-backed Attorney General Ken Paxton faces Democrat James Talarico, will be a major focus. 

Meanwhile, more than a dozen organizations are planning to rally in downtown Dallas to pull focus as top Republicans address the convention crowd. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries also announced on Friday that a four-member House delegation would be headed to Dallas to underscore the contrast between the two parties. 

“I don’t know who we have to pay to thank the Republicans for doing this at this time, but I’m happy they’re coming. I hope it gets as much airtime as possible,” said Matt Angle, founder of the Lone Star Project, a Texas-based Democratic PAC. “It gives Democrats another event to organize around and another opportunity to make the case in a convincing way.” 

Around 100 members and candidates are set to attend the Dallas convention, and the National Republican Congressional Committee (NRCC) has distributed more than 2,000 tickets, a source familiar told The Hill. The RNC has said thousands will be in attendance. Vice President Vance will cap off the first night with a speech, and Trump will deliver the closing-night keynote address. Senate Majority Leader John Thune and House Speaker Mike Johnson are among the top GOP names expected to attend, as is Senate hopeful Paxton.

“We are excited to be in Dallas for a first-of-its-kind midterm convention that will show the American people exactly what’s at stake in November,” RNC Chairman Joe Gruters said in a Thursday release previewing the event. 

Though a significant number of candidates and lawmakers have shared plans to skip the convention — citing costs, conflicts and the campaign trail — the event has been billed as a chance to highlight GOP candidates in high-stakes races and to draw a contrast with Democrats on top issues, including affordability, immigration and healthcare. 

But Democrats say they’re eager for voters to see that contrast. 

“Americans are being crushed by rising costs. Republicans don’t care—they’re in Dallas, celebrating an out of touch President whose tariffs and wars are making things worse. We’re going to hold them accountable,” said Rep. Jason Crow (D-Colo.) in a post on X. 

Crow was announced on Friday as part of the four-member House delegation that’s headed to Dallas to join in on counterprogramming, alongside Reps. Robert Garcia, (D-Calif.) Madeleine Dean (D-Pa.) and Sydney Kamlager-Dove (D-Calif.). They’ll partner with local leaders and the Texas Democratic Party on the ground. 

“While swing seat House Republicans try to hide from their record of raising costs on working families, gutting Medicaid to fund tax breaks for billionaire donors and supporting a reckless war of choice in Iran, House Democrats will be present to hold them accountable,” Jeffries said in a release.

Multiple progressive groups, labor unions and others are planning demonstrations in Dallas on Thursday. And just before Trump takes the stage on Thursday evening, a rally is set for the steps of City Hall, organized by a dozen groups including Next Generation Action Network, Powered by the People, Texas Democrats and the AFL-CIO, according to the event page. 

“Our main goal is not just simply to be a counter protest, not just to be against something. Our main goal in this protest is to be for a new future, to be for a new administration, to be for a government that is more inclusive, a little bit more ethical, a little more humane for any marginalized groups,” said Samantha Mitchell, a co-leader of Indivisible Dallas, which is involved in counterprogramming efforts. 

And while Republicans have said the convention will be a great opportunity to rev up their voters in the Lone Star State, where Paxton and Talarico are neck-and-neck for the Senate and several House seats are in play after GOP-friendly redistricting reshaped the state’s congressional maps last year, Democrats and other organizers are also hoping that the focus on those must-win contests actually fuels their own supporters. 

Indivisible, a progressive grassroots organization that started during Trump’s first term, recently announced Texas as part of its Battlegrounds program, making the red state a top target for the midterms. 

“That is huge. No one has considered Texas to be a swing state or a battleground state in three decades,” Mitchell said of the national organization’s move. “This is the first time, the first year that I’ve ever felt actually, really hopeful about the possibility that we could really swing the state, even more so than 2018 with Beto.” That year, Beto O’Rourke came within a few points of toppling Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas). 

Talarico, whose bid has surged Democratic hopes against controversy-laden Paxton, is also planning to counterprogram the convention with a statewide “Love Thy Neighbor” food drive, the campaign announced on Friday. 

“Next week, billionaire mega-donors and their puppet politicians will gather at a convention in Dallas to clink champagne glasses and toast their own corruption,” Talarico said in a release. “We’ll be doing something different.”

Decision Desk HQ’s latest polling average shows Talarico up by roughly 3 points over Paxton in the Senate race, with just two months to go until the general election. The race is considered a toss-up that narrowly favors the Democrat.

Multiple House fights in Texas could also help tip the lower chamber’s balance of power this fall, including Rep. Vicente Gonzalez’s (D-Texas) seat in the 34th Congressional District, which DDHQ considers to lean Democratic and Cook Political Report rates as a toss-up. 

Meanwhile, Trump’s approval rating is roughly 16 points underwater in the latest DDHQ averages, with just 40 percent of Americans approving of his job handling.

In Texas, which voted for Trump in each of his three runs, his approval rating was 20 points underwater as of August, according to YouGov/The Economist analysis. On top of national frustrations with high prices and the war in Iran, Texans have also been ruffled by the Trump administration’s plans for border wall construction inside Texas’s Big Bend National Park and data center builds.

But Democrats still have an uphill climb to gain ground in the longtime red stronghold this cycle. 

“There’s a sort of a little lurking challenge here, which is that, while some of the gains that Trump made among Hispanics and in urban areas in the 2024 election have receded, they haven’t receded back to historical baselines, and so Democrats and the Democratic Party, which itself is viewed very negatively here, still has a pretty steep hill to climb,” Joshua Blank, research director for the Texas Politics Project at the University of Texas at Austin, told The Hill last week.

A question for the convention is “whether or not this type of business does more to help Republicans shore up their ranks,” Blank said, “or whether it actually creates a rallying point for Democrats to reinvigorate their voters in an election in which they’re not necessarily trying to make Trump the centerpiece.”

data.title: Hegseth's pick faces competition in search for new Army secretary
data.description:
Sean Parnell, the Pentagon spokesman and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s top choice for the next Army secretary, is among at least four candidates being considered for the role, sources familiar with the process told The Hill this week. 

The field also includes at least two current officials — Marc Anderson, an assistant secretary of the Army, and Derrick Anderson, an assistant secretary of Defense — and Rep. Brian Mast (R-Fla.), an Army veteran who chairs the House Foreign Affairs Committee, sources said. 

Former Army Secretary Dan Driscoll’s departure from the Trump administration this week closed the book on an 18-month tenure in which the close ally of Vice President Vance pushed for rapid modernization of America’s largest fighting force, but repeatedly clashed behind-the-scenes with Hegseth. 

That leaves the Army without a Senate-confirmed leader on the civilian or uniformed side of operations, after Hegseth in April forced out the Army’s widely respected chief of staff, Gen. Randy George. 

On Thursday, President Trump announced that Adam Telle, the current assistant secretary of the Army for Civil Works, would be the Army’s acting secretary, catching some current and defense officials by surprise. 

Telle, an Alabama native, has spent years working in Republican offices on Capitol Hill, most recently as Sen. Bill Hagerty’s (R-Tenn.) chief of staff. 

“My previous work in the Army focused on moving at Trump Speed to deliver on one of the Army’s original missions. I will apply that same relentless focus on efficiency to how the Army mans, trains, equips, and modernizes,” Telle said in his first statement as acting Army Secretary on Friday.

It is unclear when Trump will nominate a permanent replacement for Driscoll, or whether Telle might be tapped to stay in the role for the long-term. 

Multiple sources inside and outside the Pentagon said Hegseth’s choice would be Parnell, who is also his senior advisor. 

“Every senior leader in [the] Pentagon knows that Secretary Hegseth’s preferred pick is Sean Parnell,” a senior Pentagon official said. “Sean’s well-respected across the Department, and viewed as a solid choice.” 

The Hill first reported last week that Hegseth was considering choosing Parnell for the post once Driscoll departs the administration. 

Parnell has support from multiple senior White House officials and some of the president’s outside advisers, according to four sources with knowledge of the matter. 

Parnell has been in touch with the White House about the role in recent days, one Pentagon official said this week. But a senior administration official denied it, adding that Parnell is “100 percent focused on executing the job he has now.” 

When reached for comment on Friday, the White House referred The Hill to Trump’s Thursday Truth Social post announcing Telle as acting Army secretary. 

White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles is leading the search for Driscoll’s replacement, sources told CBS News. 

Parnell, who was awarded two Bronze Stars and a Purple Heart for his service in Afghanistan, ran for Congress twice. With Trump’s endorsement, he ran for Senate in Pennsylvania, but withdrew from the race in November 2021, losing a court fight over custody of his three children, which included faced allegations of abuse by his enstranged wide. Parnell has denied the allegations. Parnell said in 2024 he had been “vindicated” and he now shares custody of all five of his children, Pentagon officials said. 

A senior government official with close knowledge of the situation told The Hill that there is “eagerness” among “most” of the Army’s three- and four-star generals to work with Parnell “given his institutional and combat experience.” 

Some officials have argued that Parnell could have a tough time being confirmed and his possible selection has already drawn rebuttals from some defense-focused Democrats. 

“Sean Parnell is Liar-in-Chief for this disastrous war in Iran. Now, Pete Hegseth wants to reward him by making him SecArmy,” Rep. Pat Ryan (D-N.Y.), a West Point graduate who sits on the House Armed Services Committee, said on Thursday. “He’s dangerously unfit for the job and we must stop him.” 

Another person floated by some in the administration is Mast, who served for 12 years in the Army and has earned multiple medals, according to two sources familiar with the matter. 

However, plucking Mast from the House would further degrade the GOP’s slim majority in the lower chamber. Mast, who currently holds a safe red seat in Florida, recently met with Hegseth, according to an administration official.  

Some within the administration fear Mast’s vocal support for Israel could rankle the MAGA base. 

“Mast has already pitched himself to everyone in DC who will listen, including Secretary Hegseth; he’s a try-hard and largely viewed as out of touch with Trump supporters,” the official said. 

Mast’s office did not respond to The Hill’s request for comment. 

Derrick Anderson, a former GOP congressional candidate in Virginia who is currently Assistant Secretary of Defense for Special Operations and Low-Intensity Conflict, is another name in the mix, according to two people familiar with the discussions.

Marc Anderson, the assistant Secretary of the Army, Financial Management and Comptroller, is also being mentioned as the potential successor to Driscoll, one person familiar with the discussions within the Pentagon said. 

Marc Anderson, who has held multiple executive leadership roles within venture capital, is not well known outside of Army circles. 

NBC News reported on Friday that Sam Brown, the undersecretary for memorial affairs at the Department of Veterans Affairs, is being floated by some in Congress and in the administration as a possible Driscoll replacement. He ran unsuccessfully twice for Senate in Nevada. 

Brown, a West Point graduate, deployed to Afghanistan as part of Operation Enduring Freedom in Kandahar, eventually medically retiring with the rank of captain.

data.title: Watchdog issues scathing report on Trump's former labor secretary
data.description:
Former Labor Secretary Lori Chavez-DeRemer allegedly fostered a “toxic, intimidating and humiliating” workplace when she led the department, a scathing watchdog report released Thursday found.

An investigation by the Labor Department’s Office of Inspector General said Chavez-DeRemer, who resigned in April, regularly drank alcohol during the workday, failed to properly report expensive gifts she had received and had an “inappropriately close and unprofessional relationship” with a member of her security detail.

The report comes nearly five months after Chavez-DeRemer left the Trump administration amid allegations of misconduct and abuse of power. She was the third member of President Trump’s Cabinet to step down.

Investigators interviewed at least 38 witnesses who consistently described the secretary’s office as “toxic,“ according to the report. Senior officials allegedly berated staffers in front of colleagues, discussed inappropriate personal matters and threatened to terminate employees.

Investigators also detailed several instances in which Chavez-DeRemer reportedly used government employees to take care of personal matters.

In one case, two employees claimed they traveled in a Labor Department vehicle to Chavez-DeRemer’s home during the workday, where they hung her dry cleaning and organized her closet. Staffers also said they were tasked with retrieving the former labor secretary’s packages and making personal purchases.

Chavez-DeRemer resigned in April, one day before investigators were scheduled to interview her, the report states. At the time, the White House said she was leaving to take a job in the private sector and praised her work leading the department.

According to a February New York Times report, the Labor Department had been investigating the former secretary and some of her top staff members for months before her departure. The probe reportedly came amid a criminal investigation into her husband, Shawn DeRemer, then accused of sexual assault against two staffers while at the agency’s headquarters.

The Times’ article cited workplace misconduct allegations against Chavez-DeRemer, a former Republican congresswoman from Oregon, similar to those mentioned in Friday’s report.

The former secretary and her husband have disputed these respective accusations.

Her attorney, Nick Oberheiden, pushed back on the inspector general’s findings Friday, telling The Washington Post the report “confirms that Secretary Chavez-DeRemer did not violate any laws.”

Keith Sonderling, who served as her deputy, took over the department on an acting basis after her departure. President Trump nominated Sonderling to permanently fill the post in June.

data.title: Vietnam veterans suing over Trump's arch seek court block ahead of groundbreaking
data.description:
The Vietnam War veterans suing over President Trump’s proposed triumphal arch are seeking an emergency court order to block the administration from pursuing its imminent plans to break ground in the Washington D.C. area.

Veterans Michael Lemmon, Shaun Byrnes, Jon Gundersen — along with architectural historian Calder Loth — filed their temporary restraining order request shortly after Interior Secretary Doug Burgum announced that project excavation would begin within the next two weeks.

Continuing their months-long legal battle with the president, the group is now claiming the Trump administration is unlawfully moving ahead with the arch without receiving necessary approval, namely that of Congress.

“Preserving Congress’s role in authorizing the design and siting of commemorative works and other structures on federal land in our national capital will ensure democratic accountability,” their lawyers wrote Friday.

The four first challenged the project in a February lawsuit attempting to halt efforts to construct the 250-foot arch, which Trump said would be the largest in the world. The National Park Service recently backed its proposed Memorial Circle location — across the Potomac River from the Lincoln Memorial.

Lemmon, Byrnes, Gundersen and Loth also arguing the large arch would obscure historical sightlines between the Lincoln Memorial, Arlington National Cemetery and Arlington House. In early August, the National Park Service (NPS) found the monument would have “adverse effects” on several historic sites as well as the skyline of the nation’s capital.

Their lawyers on Friday accused the administration of trying to move quickly enough to make the arch a “fait accompli” before U.S. District Judge Tanya Chutkan can determine whether the project is lawful.

The administration clarified the work planned for the next two weeks will consist of an archaeological survey involving four test pits to help the NPS comply with preservation requirements, rather than actual construction activity.

“This activity is not construction, or demolition in preparation for construction, of an arch,” the administration said in a legal filing submitted Friday.

Chutkan previously ordered the administration to provide 14 days’ notice before beginning construction.

The arch has received preliminary approval, but not final approval, from the National Capital Planning Commission. A historic preservation review is also underway.

data.title: Tetris suggests White House 'Build the Wall' game infringes copyright
data.description:
The Tetris Company appeared to warn the White House Friday that its new online arcade based on President Trump’s policies may constitute copyright infringement.

The site, launched Thursday, features games emulating the style of arcade classics. One of these video games, “Build the Wall,” uses mechanics that closely resemble those of Tetris. But in the White House’s version, players stack Tetris-like blocks to prevent zombies and other creatures from crossing the southern border into the U.S.

“The Tetris Company was not involved in the creation of ‘Build the Wall,’” the game company said in a statement on social media Friday, adding, “We take copyright infringement very seriously.”

A company spokesperson told Variety the White House “did not authorize or license the Tetris brand or intellectual property for the game.”

The spokesperson added that Tetris was “reviewing the matter” when asked whether the company was considering legal action.

“Build the Wall” one of five games currently available. Subtitled “Zombie Border Siege,” it instructs players to “protect the border from the coming horde.” Allowing blocks to reach the top of the screen, much like in Tetris, ends the game.

Unlike the classic video game, however, a message reading “BORDER BREACHED” appears on screen when players lose.

“At Tetris, we believe in the power of connection and bringing people together, not dividing them,” Tetris said in its social media post Friday.

The Tetris-like game is one of two games focused on the administration’s immigration policy. Another immigration-themed game titled “Rio Run” — resembling the popular “snake” video game format — depicts an agent conducting “border patrol along the Rio Grande.”

The arcade also includes “Trump Savings Tycoon,” which has players collect money for Trump Accounts; “Supply Line,” which focuses on the administration’s “Make America Healthy Again” initiative; and the White House’s spin on the popular game Flappy Bird called “Flappy Bill,” which features a bald eagle carrying legislation while it navigates obstacles above the National Mall.

data.title: Federal judge declines to halt firings of Stars and Stripes staffers
data.description:
A federal judge on Friday declined to stop the Pentagon’s termination of three Stars and Stripes staffers for alleged insubordination, ruling they were not likely to succeed in their claims that the firings violated the First Amendment.

Judge Trevor McFadden issued the decision hours after a hearing that focused on whether two of the employees were acting within the scope of their roles when they gave interviews to “CBS Sunday Morning” about the historically independent military newspaper’s editorial direction.

McFadden acknowledged in a 24-page order that the dispute was at an “early stage” but found the staffers had so far failed to demonstrate that a preliminary injunction was warranted.  

“Plaintiffs’ own pleadings and the CBS News segment suggest that they spoke as part of their official duties and not as private citizens,” the judge wrote. “They are thus unlikely to succeed on the merits of their First Amendment claim and do not demonstrate irreparable harm.”

Ousted publisher Max Lederer, Editor-in-Chief Erik Slavin and reporter Lara Korte alleged in a lawsuit filed last Thursday that the Department of Defense (DoD) is retaliating against them for speaking publicly about concerns with the military newspaper’s future editorial independence under current Pentagon leadership.

Taryn Wilgus Null, senior counsel at Democracy Defenders Fund — who filed the lawsuit on the former employees’ behalf, said in a statement that the trio’s attorneys were weighing their legal options following McFadden’s ruling.

“The judge emphasized a plaintiff’s high burden to obtain a preliminary injunction,” Null told The Hill. “While we are disappointed in the decision, we fully expect to prevail after we have an opportunity to take discovery and all the facts are revealed.”

The three staffers were issued separation notices on Aug. 21. According to court documents, officials cited “insubordination and violations of regulations based on their CBS statements” as the grounds for Slavin and Korte’s dismissal, while Lederer’s notice cited his refusal to deliver separation notices to the two other employees, among other reasons.

The publisher announced his retirement on Aug. 19, before his termination, having originally planned to step down as of Sept. 30.

The Pentagon had agreed to pause the firings until at least Friday, pending the judge’s ruling. The Hill has reached out for an update on their employment status.

Null told the judge on Friday that Slavin and Korte were speaking from a “proverbial soap box” on “matters of public concern” during their CBS appearance and were not acting on behalf of the outlet.  

The Supreme Court has previously held that a public employee’s speech is constitutionally protected when given outside the scope of their ordinary job duties even if that speech relates to their employment.

But McFadden appeared skeptical during the hearing about whether Slavin and Korte were speaking as private citizens, noting the editor-in-chief regularly gives interviews and questioning whether that made him a “de-facto” spokesperson for the paper.

“Plaintiffs’ comments were not a story, op-ed, or breaking headline that they edited or authored,” McFadden concluded in his opinion. “Indeed, Slavin and Korte’s statements were made to another media agency altogether. They were acting as spokespersons for their paper or as sources for another organization.”

The judge was also unpersuaded by claims that unfavorable coverage on the USS Lincoln’s extended deployment in the Middle East served as an “accelerant” for their firings.

The Justice Department asserted during the hearing that the decision was made weeks prior to the article being published, refuting Null’s claim that the Pentagon sat on the notices.

“It’s a red herring,” assistant U.S. attorney Brett Covington told the judge.

data.title: How are AI chatbots answering voting questions?
data.description:

The Big Story 

Nearly a third of AI chatbot replies to voting questions inaccurate, outdated: study 

Artificial intelligence chatbots are becoming a source for voters to ask questions about upcoming elections, but a new study determined nearly a third of AI-generated replies could be inaccurate or outdated. 

AP Photo/Matt Rourke, File

In a report released Thursday, researchers with the Institute for Strategic Dialogue (ISD) tested 15 different generic prompts across six AI chatbots and found 29 percent of responses were incomplete, inaccurate or outdated.

 

Generic questions included topics like mail-in voting, voter registration and important dates. 

 

Errors included misidentifying Election Day dates and showing outdated requirements and deadlines, according to the report.

 

In 16 percent of the replies, the chatbot answered correctly but did not include important information that could be useful to a voter, such as key deadlines or ways to prove identity. 

 

The models tested were Meta’s Muse Spark, xAI’s Grok 4.3, DeepSeek’s V4 Pro, OpenAI’s GPT-5.5, Anthropic’s Sonnet 4.6 and Google’s Gemini 3.5 Flash.

 

The ISD, which focuses on extremism, disinformation and online threats, tailored the prompts to 10 states with a history of electoral process changes, related legislation or election administration controversy. 

 

“As LLMs [large language models] play a larger role in shaping the information environment, the reliability and behavior of these systems will increasingly affect voter access and trust,” ISD researchers wrote.

 

 “This analysis finds that models’ overall accuracy on election process is mixed, and concerns remain over a reliance on outdated sources, overconfidence in relaying nuanced and conditional information, and performance divergences between languages,” they added.

data.title: Judge denies bail, orders jail time for ex-Kentucky Gov. Matt Bevin
data.description:
A judge on Friday ordered former Kentucky Gov. Matt Bevin (R) to serve 60 days in jail without bond after he was arrested on an outstanding warrant in a child support case involving his estranged wife.

“He has over and over again demonstrated a complete disregard and utter disrespect for this court,” Judge Angela Johnson said during the Friday afternoon hearing. “You have shown this court that you are not going to do what you are ordered to do because you don’t think it should be this way.”

A warrant for his arrest was issued in June after the former governor failed to produce court-ordered financial documents.

Bevin was arrested Thursday in Paris, Ky., on the set of a Christmas movie where he was working as an extra. The Bourbon County Sheriff’s Office said it had received a tip that he was participating in the film project.

Sheriff Tony Asbury said in a press release that Bevin was “very cooperative” during his arrest.

Bevin’s attorneys argued the contempt order was not appropriate because he was unable to do what the court asked of him.

The warrant was tied to Bevin’s failure to provide financial documents in a child support dispute involving his adopted son, Jonah Bevin, who is seeking retroactive support.

John Helmers, an attorney for Jonah Bevin, accused the former governor of actively avoiding the court in Friday’s hearing, including by being on the set of a movie rather than complying with the court order.

“These are the same rules that apply to every citizen, everyone in the state of Kentucky,” Helmers said.

“The sad reality is that adoption is supposed to be forever,” Jonah Bevin said in a statement issued Friday. “And this makes it clear that my parents haven’t felt that kind of love for me in a long time.”

Bevin served as Kentucky governor from 2015 to 2019, before narrowly losing reelection to current Gov. Andy Beshear (D).

data.title: Pennsylvania infant's death confirmed to have been caused by measles
data.description:
Click in for more news from The Hill
{beacon}

Healthcare

Healthcare

 

The Big Story 

Pennsylvania infant confirmed to have died from measles 

Following vocal skepticism from federal health officials, one of the two suspected measles deaths reported in Pennsylvania last month has been confirmed as being caused by the virus. 

Sean Rayford, Getty Images

Lancaster County coroner Stephen Diamantoni confirmed on Friday that a 6-week-old infant died of measles in Pennsylvania. According to Diamantoni, the child was born with Amish lethal microcephaly, a rare genetic condition that can cause respiratory infections. 

 

This confirmation comes after several Trump administration officials openly questioned whether the deaths had even occurred.  

 

Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services Administrator Mehmet Oz questioned whether the cause of death was measles while Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. suggested the deaths could have been entirely fabricated by Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro (D). 

 

The confusion stemmed from Pennsylvania state officials reporting two “measles-associated” deaths but Lancaster County Commissioner Josh Parsons (R) saying he was not aware of any reported deaths from measles and questioned where Shapiro got his information. 

 

Kennedy called Shapiro after the announcement and their apparently contentious conversation bled over into a heated back-and-forth online. 

 

Shapiro responded to news of the confirmation on social media. Kennedy reportedly asked that the Pennsylvania deaths be removed from the CDC’s official national tally. 

 

‘Last week, the Pennsylvania Department of Health reported our Commonwealth’s first two measles-associated deaths in 35 years,” Shapiro wrote.  

 

“Then, instead of listening to the real doctors and public health experts, RFK chose to sow doubt, play politics, direct the CDC not to acknowledge these deaths, and even accuse me of fabricating these tragedies,” he added. “That led to a firestorm of conspiracy theories that denied these families’ pain, invaded their privacy, and undermined public health.”
